articles.title: Astra MkII on the MiG-29UPG: what a 200 km missile does and doesn’t fix
articles.text:
An effective beyond-visual-range shot requires two things to happen at the same time: the shooter’s radar must hold a fire-control track on the target, and the missile must have the kinematic reach. The effective launch range is therefore the smaller of the two — the radar track range and the missile’s maximum range. Radar range scales with target radar cross-section as range proportional to RCS to the power one-quarter.
This is why the Astra MkII’s headline range is only half the story. The missile can fly 200 km but the Zhuk-M2E can only track a fighter-sized target out to roughly 76-107 km. Self-cued, the MiG is capped by its radar; cued by an AWACS over datalink — the Astra MkII has two-way AWACS datalink the radar limit is bypassed and the missile’s full range becomes usable.
Track ranges below are the detection range scaled to each target’s RCS and to the fraction at which a fire-control track holds. Every AESA opponent tracks the MiG-29UPG (5 sq m) further out than the MiG tracks it.
Head-on engagements, 40,000 runs each, with the side that fires first forcing the other defensive. The R-77 baseline shows what the Astra MkII change
It changes lethality and, with cueing, reach; against the JF-17 the effect is stark; the same 76 km launch that the R-77 makes a marginal shot (P(kill) about 0.18) becomes a strong one for the Astra (about 0.48) (76 km is well inside the Astra’s much larger no-escape zone while the JF-17’s own PL-15E shot, fired at its 136 km limit, is a low-probability one) alone moves the MiG from a near-even exchange to a decisive edge.
Detection is not changed, however; the Zhuk-M2E remains a mechanically-scanned radar and every AESA opponent still detects and tracks the MiG before it tracks them. Against the J-10C and J-16, with their 200 km domestic PL-15 and better radars, AWACS cueing brings the MiG to parity at best (the J-10C retains a measurable edge as its own 153 km track gives it a higher-quality shot than the MiG’s 200 km maximum-range launch).
Bottom line for the air-superiority question is that the Astra MkII puts the MiG-29UPG back in the fight as a lethal shooter inside a network and gives it genuine standoff against the JF-17. It does not, on its own, overturn the sensor advantage of the J-10C or J-16. To close that gap requires the radar (the Uttam Mk2 AESA now planned for the MiG-29K; same logic applies to the MiG-29UPG).

articles.title: NTT Global Data Centers weighs the price tag of not building fast enough
articles.text: The next 200-megawatt data center permitted in your county probably won't look like the buildings you remember from a decade ago. It will occupy the footprint of two or three football fields and draw more power than most nearby industrial parks combined. It will also likely trigger a town hall meeting before the first pad is poured. That collision between AI-driven demand and physical reality is what NTT Global Data Centers set out to quantify in its new AI Stress Test Report. The report models three growth trajectories through 2030 and stress-tests each against the constraints operators hit, such as land availability, water consumption, specialized labor and more. The middle (baseline) scenario projects annual demand growth of about 23 percent, which pencils out to roughly $3.8 trillion of additional investment in digital infrastructure. Ramp to the accelerated case and the figure climbs to $5.7 trillion. Bruno Berti, CTO at NTT Global Data Centers, notes that he has watched the size envelope stretch beyond recognition. "We used to build ten-megawatt buildings, smaller buildings, to support some of these applications," says Berti. "But now we're building buildings that are hundreds of megawatts, double the size, sizes of two, maybe sometimes three football fields." Why permitting became the choke point Ask most operators what will bottleneck AI infrastructure and you'll hear GPUs, transformers, switchgear. NTT Global Data Centers’ stress test suggests something more mundane: paperwork, planning and process. Power availability and deployment timelines, not fiber capacity, are the gating factors in the scenarios modeled. Berti puts it plainly: it doesn't matter how quickly you can get GPUs if you can't get a permit to put them anywhere. That reframes the strategy question. Berti argues against a "build, baby, build" reflex, preferring a portfolio approach that treats capacity expansion as a system-wide coordination problem rather than a land race. The misconceptions that stall projects Two objections come up in almost every community consultation, according to Berti: data centers waste water, and they steal power from the grid. Both are misconceptions and come from an older generation of facilities. Modern designs, he says, use liquid cooling technology, which removes heat more effectively, eliminating excess water waste. Additionally, operators plan the new class of hundred-megawatt-plus sites in partnership with utilities years in advance, often with on-site solar, wind or other renewable generation that can help stabilize the grid rather than drain it. His conclusion is blunt: transparency builds trust. So, the industry has to stop treating what it does as a secret and start to build that trust through education and partnership if it wants the permits it will need through the decade to turn capacity into reliable AI infrastructure that can benefit communities, policymakers and businesses alike. articles.title: NewSpace Tests RATO Booster on Sheshnag-150 Lottering Munition for Canister Launches
articles.text:
NewSpace’s GryphonWorks carried out successfully testing a rocket-assisted take-off (RATO) booster for its Sheshnag-150 one-way attack (OWA) drone, according to an NewSpace Research and Technologies (NRT) announcement. The company described the trial as a first for an indigenous designed, developed and manufactured (IDDM) long-range strike asset.
The test is related to the crucial requirement for any long-range unmanned aerial vehicle to provide enough initial thrust to get off the ground. A RATO booster provides additional thrust needed for the take-off, enabling an aircraft to operate even from an environment that would not be appropriate for a standard runway-assisted launch. The Sheshnag-150 integrates cutting-edge autonomous and swarm technology specifically designed to meet India’s operational needs. In Sheshnag-150, the range is approximately 1000-1200km, with a capacity of 25-40kg of explosive.
The RATO trial therefore represents a particular technical milestone, since RATO booster is an bolt-on system that provides a short, high-thrust burn that accelerates the munition out of the canister up to flying speed and a safe climb angle, then it burns out and separates, the wings open up and the sustainer takes over for the loiter phase. A RATO launch needs only a zero-length rail to guide the vehicle, a footprint roughly the size of the munition itself, versus the much larger rig one needs for a catapult or pneumatic launcher
NewSpace Research and Technologies (NRT) Team congratulated its GryphonWorks team on the test, while the announcement itself suggested that the trial represented a significant milestone for India’s indigenously developed long-range strike capability. The announcement did not state the location of the test, its timing, the details of the booster used, or how many trials had taken place.
India’s Sheshnaag-150 is expected to eventually incorporate a visual navigation system, enabling operations in environments where satellite-based navigation is disrupted or denied a growing concern in high-intensity conflicts
India has seen increasing interest in the development of indigenous unmanned strike systems, which can provide expeditionary armed forces with one-way alternative to traditional pilot-in-control aviation. The combat utility of such systems would be defined by their operational range, payload capacity, navigation capability, resistance to electronic warfare, and ability to launch and operate effectively in the chosen environment. Such capabilities were not demonstrated by the RATO trial, which only addressed one element of the aircraft’s performance.

articles.title: Uncle Scam Wants You … to cough up your cash and personal data, FBI warns ahead of midterms
articles.text: The FBI is once again warning US citizens to be on the lookout for the scams that are so often rife around election season. With November’s midterms fast approaching, the FBI said scammers are known to use the names, imagery, and slogans of high-profile candidates for a range of frauds. These are often related to making donations and selling merchandise, but can also be geared toward stealing personal data for use in follow-on scams. And of course, more recently, fraudsters’ efforts can be all the more convincing given the rise in AI use and deepfake technology, which can also be used to more accurately imitate the likenesses of candidates and other officials. Campaign investment pool schemes are among the four big frauds the FBI wants the public to watch out for over the next few weeks. These involve scammers convincing their marks to pay into a campaign pool, which ostensibly pays out to all of those who donated after the candidate wins. More commonly, these types of pooled investment scams are based on collective investments into stocks and other appreciating assets. The FBI did not provide details about these campaign pools’ investment incentives or how victims are supposedly able to increase their stake by donating to the cause, but did say that no genuine campaign donations appreciate over time. Another common donation-based scam to be wary of is the one that convinces victims to fund a fake political action committee (PAC), one that collects supporters’ cash and promises to hand it to their favored party or candidate. Instead of forwarding money to a specific political campaign, however, the scammers pocket it all for themselves. Fraudsters are also known for claiming to sell merchandise related to political campaigns – orders that ultimately go unfulfilled. These constitute non-delivery scams, which rank in the top five genres of internet cons, according to the Internet Crime Complaint Center’s (IC3) most recent annual report. The same report put phishing at the number one spot in that same list, and the classic cyberattack features on the FBI’s list of midterm-related scams, too. Creating a sense of urgency, scammers will text victims claiming they have not yet registered to vote, and asking them to follow a link to a webpage where they can enter their details and complete the process, which of course leads to identity theft. While the FBI doesn’t include this detail in its advisory, Texans should be especially wary of these communication attempts given the recent computer issues that led to a massive backlog in registration applications. As of September 22, 226, around 600,000 applications were allegedly in limbo after a website flaw failed to record voters’ intentions to vote, and therefore did not receive registration forms from the Texas Secretary of State (SOS), according to a lawsuit [PDF] filed by voter registration organizations last week. However, spokesperson for the SOS’ office Alicia Pierce told USA Today that the backlog was only in the tens of thousands and that as of this week it was all-clear. Scammers may nevertheless continue to capitalize on the public awareness of the backlog when devising the lures for their phishing campaigns. The feds advised the public to be wary of these kinds of communications, and verify all political organizations, such as PACs, via the government’s election commission website. Although some scam PACs can appear on the website as registered, you can usually discern the suspicious ones when they report high expenses for matters such as consulting, fundraising, and other admin costs. The FBI's advisory follows separate action taken by X, which on Wednesday evening warned that influence campaigns originating from Iran, Russia, and China were targeting US voters, amplifying content across the political spectrum. The social media platform responded by nuking more than 13,000 accounts linked to the foreign interference attempts. ®

articles.title: Manipur Ambush Leaves Kuki Woman Dead, Two Civilians Missing
articles.text:
A middle-aged Kuki tribal woman was killed and two other civilians went missing after suspected militants ambushed two motorcycles in Manipur’s Kamjong district on Thursday evening, officials said.
A police official, quoting local villagers, said that four civilians travelling on two motorcycles to Phaikoh to purchase essential commodities were ambushed between Phaikoh and Molvailup.
The woman, identified as Hatneimkim Haokip, died on the spot, while her husband escaped unhurt, the official added.
The two other civilians remain missing, and their whereabouts are unknown.
Security personnel, along with villagers, have launched search operations to trace the missing persons.
Various organisations, including the Kuki Inpi Manipur (KIM), have strongly condemned the killing.
In a statement, KIM Secretary for Information and Publicity Janghaolun Haokip accused the National Socialist Council of Nagalim (Isak-Muivah) of carrying out the attack and alleged that the outfit had repeatedly targeted defenceless civilians, particularly women and children.
Describing the incident as a grave violation of humanitarian principles, he said that the alleged attacks on vulnerable civilians and villagers were unacceptable and must be condemned in the strongest possible terms.
The KIM also held the state and Central governments responsible for what it described as a breakdown of law and order that had allowed insurgent groups to operate with impunity.
Accusing the authorities of indecision and failure to take decisive action, Haokip demanded an immediate and comprehensive security operation to identify and apprehend those responsible for Haokip’s killing and trace the two missing civilians.
He said that mere assurances were no longer sufficient and called for concrete action to ensure the safety of civilians and bring the perpetrators to justice.
The KIM expressed condolences to the bereaved family and said that the organisation stood in solidarity with them during their hour of grief.
It warned that failure to take immediate and tangible steps to bring the perpetrators to justice, locate the missing civilians and ensure the protection of innocent people could lead to public unrest and further escalation of tensions.
(IANS)

articles.title: MARTAC USVs Gain Real-Time Machine Vision from SEA.AI
articles.text:
MARTAC has integrated SEA.AI machine vision on its unmanned surface vessels. The system classifies contacts in real time at the sensor, so USVs understand their surroundings without anyone watching a video feed.

SEA.AI press release

MARTAC has integrated SEA.AI maritime machine vision on its unmanned surface vessels (USVs). The system classifies vessels and objects in real time at the sensor, so a USV operating far beyond its operators’ line of sight gets usable situational awareness without anyone watching a video feed.

MARTAC, a Florida-based manufacturer of high-performance autonomous maritime platforms, selected SEA.AI as part of its sensor integration architecture. The integration covers ISR, security, and patrol mission profiles. SEA.AI announced the partnership with MARTAC on 13 October 2026.

Why radar and AIS leave a gap in maritime domain awareness

Radar resolves a contact’s position and radar cross-section, but not what the contact is. AIS is voluntary, routinely manipulated, and missing on any platform that chooses not to broadcast.

In today’s grey zone environment, these limits carry operational weight because threats are designed to exploit them: dark vessels, spoofed identities, and fast-attack craft that look like surrounding traffic until the moment they act.

How SEA.AI turns a camera feed into actionable information

Electro-optical and thermal cameras have long been part of maritime sensing. The weak point is what happens after the image is captured. On an autonomous platform, a conventional camera produces video, and that video is useless without an analyst watching it continuously.

SEA.AI runs AI inference at the sensor level. Its electro-optical and thermal system classifies each contact in real time and outputs vessel or object type, heading, and proximity as actionable information, with no human review of imagery.

For a USV beyond visual range of its operators, this separates genuine situational awareness from a data stream nobody has time to interpret.

Built for missions beyond the operator’s reach

In May 2026, MARTAC’s T38 Devil Ray completed a record 8-day fully autonomous mission off the coast of California. It navigated multiple real surface contacts in open-ocean conditions, without crew or escort, more than 400 nautical miles from shore.

At that range and in Sea State 5 conditions, no remote operator can review imagery in time. The vessel has to detect and understand its environment on its own, and that is the capability SEA.AI brings.

“We built SEA.AI in 2018 around a conviction that the camera alone was never going to be enough at sea. The intelligence had to be in the system, not in a person watching a screen somewhere. That requirement has only become more urgent as autonomous platforms move from trials into operational deployment.”

Marcus Warrelmann, CEO, SEA.AI

“Operators have sensors, platforms, and more data than their teams can process. What we add to a MARTAC vessel is not another feed to monitor, it is a system that watches, understands, and reports. This partnership with MARTAC puts that capability where it matters: on proven platforms, in real missions.”

Diogo ArredaManaging Director US, SEA.AI

“Our platforms are built to carry whatever sensors the mission requires, and we evaluate every integration on one basis: does it make the vessel more operationally capable? SEA.AI’s machine vision, that classifies contacts autonomously and in real time, is a direct solution for closing a real gap. That is why it is on our platforms.”

Jim HarveyChief Technology Officer, MARTAC

SEA.AI machine vision, proven at sea since 2018

SEA.AI pioneered maritime machine vision in 2018. Its systems combine optical and thermal sensors with artificial intelligence to detect what radar and AIS often miss: persons overboard, marine mammals, unlit vessels, small craft, containers, semi-submerged logs, and other floating hazards, day and night, in real time.

articles.title: Su-57E: Why Russia Wants Indian Order Amid Limited Production and Export Demand
articles.text:
The Su-57E’s revival of interest in India sales mirrors another issue plaguing the programme – it requires production scale, which Moscow may have limited ability to supply for its own air force. India provides the opportunity for a big order, domestic manufacturing and a long-term industrial partnership. However, despite the growing offers from India, New Delhi has not yet agreed to purchase the 5th generation fighter.
According to information provided, Russia has signed a contract in June 2019 for purchase of 76 Su-57 aircraft for its army and they will be delivered till 2027-28. The order is still low compared to the F-35 made by the American company and the Chinese J-20. Two of these airframe losses are reported – one in 2019 and one in 2026 – adding to the difficulty to determine the number of effective aircraft on hand.
Actual deliveries of aircraft are not certain. According to the information provided in the supplied data, the operational fleet was projected to be between 20 and 30 aircraft by early 2026 and around 20 aircraft on service with four to five in production. Meanwhile, Russian sources have put the deliveries orders higher, with batches delivered between 2023 and 25 and yet another in September 2026. The difference makes it hard to accurately estimate the production rate of the Programme.
Production capacity is just a part of the problem. Russia is living with sanctions and the stresses of war and continues to rely upon the Su-34 and Su-35 for its combat aircraft needs. These conflicting demands restrict the capacity to produce more Su-57s. A big order from India may help keep the manufacturing line going and help defray development costs over a larger number of customers, but it will also put more pressure on an industrial system already under strain.
Moscow has another reason to go for India, courtesy of the export record. The delivered material lists only Algeria as a confirmed foreign buyer, where a US$2 billion order for about 14 aircraft is reported. The first two were reportedly delivered in late 2025 and have been spotted flying in Algeria by early 2026. The Russian authorities have also mentioned other export orders, but there have been no public confirmations of the customers and volumes of these orders.
In the backdrop of this, Indian Potential order is particularly appealing. Russia has reportedly offered to supply technology transfer and access to source code for mission systems, as well as to supply local production of approximately 100 Su-57E aircraft. Other offers have included an assembly order of 36-60 aircraft, an order for two squadrons to be produced in collaboration with others, and some technology for the engine. The width of these offers indicates that Moscow is willing to make significant concessions to obtain a big market.
But the export problems of the aircraft are not just due to production. Issues of stealth, U.S. sanctions, and delivery dates also impact potential customers. Technical comparisons between the different models that are flying around in public commentary, such as estimates of radar cross-section are not directly comparable without consistent conditions of measurement and should not be used as definitive statements of combat effectiveness.
India, however, has other priorities. In July 2026, Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh stated that India was not interested in ordering any other variant of the Sukhoi. New Delhi is focused on the Su-30MKI upgrade programme, more Rafale buying and the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), which is still a long way down the road.
The Su-57 pitch was reportedly renewed during the BRICS summit in September 2026 by Russian President Vladimir Putin and no agreement was reached. With that, Moscow has not yet secured the big deal that will help to expand the plane’s production facilities, and India has the chance to go ahead with its own fighter project.

articles.title: British watchdog seeks tougher terms around Microsoft's dominance of business software
articles.text: The UK's competition watchdog wants to designate Microsoft with strategic market status (SMS) in business software, allowing the regulator it to intervene to level the playing field, and says it is considering other areas for investigation. Regulators around the world are watching to see what the UK decides in this case, with bodies such as the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and the European Commission mulling similar actions. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is opening a consultation on whether to tag the Redmond software giant with strategic market status in respect of its portfolio of business software applications. This follows an investigation the regulator started back in May into Microsoft’s software portfolio including Word, Excel, Outlook, PowerPoint and Teams, plus its security, server and operating systems. The watchdog is also probing whether Microsoft enjoys a position of “substantial and entrenched market power” through the suite of software that could be seen as stifling competition and harming buyer choice. It lays out its proposed decision in a document [PDF] and is inviting comments that must be submitted by November 13. The CMA will make its final decision by February 13, 2027. Bargain spotter The CMA makes it clear the company holds a strong position in each of the five areas it investigated (personal computer operating systems, productivity software suites, security software, server operating systems and relational database management systems), and that customers face barriers when switching providers – limiting their choice and weakening the ability of other software developers to offer rival products. Its proposal document notes Microsoft has been by far the largest provider of business software in the UK for decades. It finds that many customers view Microsoft's portfolio as a unified software environment, forming an end-to-end, integrated stack which makes for easier technical integration between products, with discounted pricing for buying whole bundles of applications together. This makes customers less likely to adopt products from alternative providers that may offer similar or superior functionality, as doing so would duplicate licensing costs for products already in their Microsoft bundle, the CMA says. “Organizations should be able to choose the products that work best for them, switch provider when they want to and combine services from different suppliers. We want to ensure businesses have the freedom to choose how they use Microsoft’s products alongside alternatives,” said CMA chief exec Sarah Cardell. Finding that the criteria for SMS designation are met would not imply or assume wrongdoing on Microsoft’s part, the regulator stresses. A separate document [PDF] spells out the potential interventions that the CMA could make. These include ensuring that Microsoft’s technical design choices do not restrict the ability to use other providers; that commercial arrangements (like bundling) do not limit effective competition; and preventing Microsoft from using its market power in business software to distort competition in adjacent activities, such as cloud services.  Rivals back licensing scrutiny Cloud providers previously complained that Microsoft's licensing terms make it more costly for companies to deploy Windows Server instances and services such as SQL Server on non-Microsoft clouds. The proposed SMS designation grew out of the CMA’s investigations into whether the big global players were having a negative impact on the cloud services market in the UK. This largely fizzled out with the watchdog securing undertakings from Microsoft and Amazon Web Services (AWS) that they would work to reduce barriers to switching between clouds and operating multi-cloud deployments. In an update, the CMA says that more can be done to address barriers to switching between cloud providers and using multiple cloud services, and it will continue to work with AWS and Microsoft to address them. It also says it its looking into whether customers can freely choose the best AI tools, and whether alternative AI providers have a level playing field to compete against Copilot. In a statement sent to The Register, Microsoft said it does not share the CMA’s views in its proposed decision on business software solutions. “All our products - including Copilot - are open and interoperable, giving customers the ability to use them alongside competing services and choose solutions that work best for them at attractive prices. We will continue engaging constructively to ensure UK customers and businesses carry on benefiting from robust competition,” a spokesperson told us. However, some pressure groups were quick to signal their approval. The Browser Choice Alliance said it welcomes the CMA’s proposed decision, adding that: “BCA members have long experienced how Microsoft leverages its market power from Windows and productivity software to push users towards its Edge browser, even where they’re trying to use an alternative.” The Open Cloud Coalition, which counts Google as a member, said: “Microsoft’s restrictive software licensing practices distort competition in the cloud, harm choice, and increase costs. This once-in-a-generation opportunity to end these practices can strengthen competition and lower customer costs, if the CMA acts quickly and decisively.” ®

articles.title: Want your AI chats to stay private? Brave TEEs up end-to-end encryption
articles.text: Brave Software has set up a secure space so those using its browser can converse with the company's AI assistant in private. At a time when AI agents like Meta's Muse ask for extensive access to personal information, and AI companies repurpose conversations for training, this amounts to swimming against the tide. Following up on an experiment launched last November to implement a confidential channel for LLM conversations with the help of NEAR AI's trusted execution environment (TEE), the browser maker has connected its Leo AI assistant to Z.ai's GLM 5.3 Flash under the protection of end-to-end encryption. The result is that Brave users can submit a prompt to Leo that gets encrypted on-device and sent over the network using Oblivious HTTP, a protocol for separating network requests from associated content. Brave's AI Gateway forwards the encrypted query to the TEE without passing along the user's IP address. After Brave verifies the enclave's attestation, the browser encrypts the query using a key bound to the TEE. The TEE decrypts the request, runs it through the AI model, and sends back an encrypted response that gets decrypted by the receiving browser. "In 2014, I argued in 'Trust but Verify' that users shouldn't have to place blind trust in the software they rely on," said Brendan Eich, co-founder and CEO of Brave, in a statement. "They should be able to verify it; this is a user-first principle. AI has raised the stakes, yet too much of it still runs on 'trust me bro' promises, often at the user's expense." NEAR AI's confidential AI pipeline is built with Intel TDX and Nvidia Confidential Compute. It includes end-to-end encryption that keeps Brave from knowing what was asked and NEAR AI from knowing who did the asking during the network hop. Data isolation prevents the prompt or response from being read during processing. Responses are signed in the TEE and there's attestation so users can confirm there's no model bait-and-switch. Leo's GLM 5.3 Flash brain may be isolated in this scenario, but Brave's AI bot can still conduct searches from within the TEE via the Brave Search API's LLM context endpoint. And any searches done this way transit via the TEE rather than the user's browser, which keeps the user's IP address out of the picture. The implementation isn't quite complete: Brave intends to work on moving the verification step into the browser and to publish a log of TEE keys, and to provide enclave attestation for exact model weights loaded into memory, among other things. Brave is not the only company trying to make AI less of a data exposure risk. Apple, AWS, Google, Nvidia, and Microsoft all have some form of private cloud compute infrastructure for AI. Then there's Prem AI, which promises encrypted inference, not to mention providers advertising zero data retention, which isn't as verifiable. One way to ensure privacy while using AI is to run inference on local hardware using an open weight model, assuming the model and the machine running it haven't been compromised. ®

articles.title: F-35 Sale to India Is for Pentagon to Decide, Says US Envoy
articles.text:
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor has refrained from giving a direct answer on whether Washington could offer the F-35 stealth fighter to India, but called for the Pentagon to address the question. Gor said in an interview with NDTV’s Vishnu Som on 15 October that the deployment of American F-35s at Tarang Shakti 2026 is a testament to Washington’s trust in India and its significance as a defence partner.
When asked if India is considering the fifth-generation fighter, Gor pointed to the US Department of Defense, also known as the Pentagon. He didn’t say that a selling offer had been made or whether negotiations were ongoing.
But I will tell you there are incredible things happening which are already happening,” said Gor, referring to the broader defence link between the two countries. He said India has more military drills with the United States than any other, and pointed out that Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of US Indo-Pacific Command, recently visited India.
Gor specifically highlighted India’s deployment of F-35 fighter jets in Tarang Shakti, the Indian Air Force’s multi-lateral air exercise at Jodhpur. His presence was an indicator of the confidence in New Delhi that the “F-35s” do not go into any country except trusted partner countries.
The exercise took place from 26 September to 12 October 2026 and involved the U.S. and six other foreign nations. F-35 Lightning II, which is an advanced combat jet, was also among the list of jets that participated in the exercise along with other platforms such as Rafale and F-16. This exercise was supposed to improve the interoperability between the two air forces, facilitate a professional exchange and provide both air forces with practice in working together.
But Ambassador’s statements are not a sign of offering F-35 to India. His answer doesn’t confirm nor rule out a potential sale, delivery date or acquisition talks with the Pentagon. That’s significant because during the conclusion of Tarang Shakti, Indian Air Force Chief Air Chief Marshal A.P Singh had stated that the U.S. has not made any official offer to sell the F-35 to India. The remarks came after the plane was used in the exercise for the first time, and gave a sense of the disconnect between public comments on a possible sale and a real procurement proposal.
The F-35 debate in India is part of the larger discussion on requirements of next generation fighter, access to technology and even the dichotomy between what they already have in the pipeline and what they are looking for. With the plane being deployed, it’s a means for Washington to prove its military commitment without its having to make a purchase.

articles.title: Capita set to miss legal deadline on 93,000 civil servants' pension fixes, claims union
articles.text: Capita is set to leave 93,000 pension cases waiting for legally required corrections after its disastrous takeover of the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS), according to the UK’s largest civil service union. The outsourcing biz took over the scheme in December 2025, offering its 1.7 million members a glitchy online portal and a service that has buckled under demand. Thousands have since had trouble receiving payments and or getting their details updated. In a statement, the PCS union - which has around 170,000 members - said the Cabinet Office had confirmed it would miss the March 2027 deadline for cases arising from the McCloud judgment, which found that changes to public service pension schemes unlawfully discriminated against younger members. The ruling required the government to review and, where necessary, correct pension benefits for the affected period. Around 73,000 retired or deceased members and 20,000 deferred members are still waiting, the union said. The deadline to complete these changes was set for March 2025, but in January this year, the government said it would extend the deadline to March 31, 2027. Capita was due to start the work when it took over the CSPS, but PCS claimed the outsourcer was stuck in the design stage it started in July. PCS general secretary Fran Heathcote said: “These people are waiting for legally required corrections to their pensions, yet Capita has still not begun processing the outstanding cases. We cannot even give members reliable information about when their pensions will be corrected. Capita’s mess continues to pile up at the expense of members. I don’t know what more the Government needs to see before it finally says enough is enough.” The Register has asked Capita and the Cabinet Office to comment. Capita won the seven-year, £239 million contract to oversee the CSPS in November 2023, taking over from MyCSP, which ran the scheme on behalf of the Cabinet Office under a £238 million contract that was first agreed in 2012. The Register revealed its troubled launch in December last year. Since then, it has hit the lives of civil servants waiting for their pensions, some of whom have been “left struggling to make ends meet at a pivotable point in their life, causing them significant distress and anxiety,” Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair of a parliamentary spending watchdog, said in July. Capita’s original contract award for CSPS details “provision of options and benefits calculations resulting from McCloud judgment”. However, in a written statement to Parliament in March this year, Satvir Kaur, then Parliamentary Secretary for the Cabinet Office, said the £239 million contract with Capita covers the day-to-day management of the Civil Service Pension Scheme, but does not include the specific cost of resolving the remaining McCloud remedy cases. The government is paying for that work through a separate, dedicated Capita-run project, Remedy Project 7, at an additional cost of £45 million, said Kaur.®

Following the Paper Trail: What DRDO’s Public Research Output Quietly Reveals
articles.text:
When a major DRDO programme announcement is made, it usually comes in a fully formed manner, such as successful test flight, induction of a new system, formal RFP etc. One thing that rarely gets documented in a systematic manner in Indian defence media is the gradual process of publishing research papers, giving talks at conferences, and filing patents on a particular technical subject – a process that typically takes years to occur – that precedes the official announcement of any programme on a particular subject. It is a tried and tested open source intelligence method which is widely adopted for Western defence analysts to monitor Chinese and Russian military research agendas, and must be used more systematically to the Indian military’s research output than the country’s defence journalism is currently.
The logic behind this is very simple. Research output at the laboratory level, published in journals of the Indian government research agencies (such as the relevant IIITs and IIMs) or their affiliated engineering conferences and in international journals on materials or aerospace research and development, is a much more difficult-to-smear-or-spin type of output, and a more accurate indicator of research investment in that area where the researchers are truly active. Say, a string of published research studies over several years and in several laboratories into, for example, hypersonic thermal protection materials, or a string of published research studies over several years and in several laboratories into something else, like quantum sensing applications or directed-energy weapon components, is a more meaningful indicator of an institution’s genuine interest than a single ministerial statement about future intentions in the same area.
This approach has to be more systematic than individual journalists can possibly have the bandwidth for, and means cross-referencing lists of publications available on the public websites of the DRDO laboratories, the IIT or IISc materials-science or aerospace departments, and patent applications filed at the Indian patent office by institutions associated with defence research. Such tracking, if done correctly, can reveal real-world forward-looking signs of shifts in India’s priority areas for defence research, months or even years before the official announcement or, worse, unverifiable insider reports, which can be misleading.
While there are limits to what this technique can ethically be used to show responsibly, they should be clarified, not glossed over for brevity’s sake, or to make for a more dramatic story. Published scientific research is not necessarily the result of a funded acquisition programme, and the time from an initial idea for a weapons programme to the delivery of a fielded system can be many years, or in many significant examples, never come to fruition. So a systematic research-trail tracking exercise is more aptly viewed as a means of determining where to seek informed questions of DRDO and MoD officials than as a means to replace actual confirmed reporting and any conclusions that are drawn from it should be presented as such not as programme intelligence.
What this publication can do, and what would truly be original and exclusive research outputs tracking rather than a one-time job, would be to over time, cross-check publications, patents and formal programme announcements as they are made to create a track record as to how effective this leading indicator of publication works for Indian defence research specifically. That is a much more serious, original defence journalism than the kind of “cynical” reporting that Indian defence media does on official announcements after the fact, and it is at the level that other defence-analysis publications in the West have developed when it comes to tracking Chinese and Russian research priorities.

It is reported that four US Air Force F-35A Lightning II fighter aircraft, which took part in Tarang Shakti 2026 at the Jodhpur Air Force Station, are now heading back to their deployment sites in the Pacific having stayed in India for about three weeks. According to open-source flight-tracking data, several KC-135R/T Stratotanker aircraft are providing support for this movement.

The pattern of tanker operations shows the kind of logistical assistance needed in order to transport combat aircraft over long distances from overseas exercise sites to their home bases or to their forward-deployment bases.
By means of aerial refuelling, fighters are able to increase their range between landing points, and the positioning of tankers together with support aircraft helps to enable these complicated international movements.
The fact that the F-35As have returned marks the end of a significant stage in US involvement in Tarang Shakti 2026. Since the exercise involved foreign aircraft and personnel, it gave the taking part air forces the chance to carry out operations in a multinational setting. articles.title: Microsoft bringing Defender to Linux desktops. Repeat: Microsoft bringing Defender to Linux desktops
articles.text: It might not be the Year of the Linux Desktop yet, but it could be the Year of Corporate Compliance on the Linux Desktop as Microsoft releases Defender for Linux Workstations. The product is an extension of Microsoft's existing Defender for Endpoint. According to the Windows behemoth, it brings "enterprise-grade protection, detection, vulnerability management and response capabilities to Linux workstations." Linux desktop users will get services including Defender's anti-virus functionality. The penguin-primed product also has management tools for inventory and security settings, as well as device isolation. "The result," said Microsoft, "is broader Linux protection, delivered through the tools and processes security teams already trust." The release is currently in public preview and requires the standalone Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Plan 2 or Microsoft 365 E5 and E7. Support is based on the underlying Linux distribution and kernel version, with RHEL, CentOS, Ubuntu LTS, SUSE Linux Enterprise Server, and Oracle Linux among others on the list. There's no separate desktop agent to deploy or maintain. Defender works the same way as it does on Linux servers, so administrators shouldn't face many challenges. End users… well… that's another story. As enterprises gain visibility into Linux workstations alongside the rest of their endpoint estate, some friction is possible and it won't be technical. For some, compliance through Microsoft's tooling is anathema, no matter how penguin-friendly it claims to be nowadays. As for the why, we're told it's simple business and customer demand. Microsoft noted that more developers are using Linux desktops, which in turn makes them more attractive to attackers. "As Linux adoption expands beyond the datacenter, organizations need a consistent approach to protecting Linux wherever it is used," Microsoft said. The idea of Microsoft Defender being able to peer at Linux desktops may alarm some, but Microsoft announced  Defender ATP for Linux back in 2020. The better question is: why has it taken so long? We'd also quibble with the premise "As more developers begin to use Linux desktops." Many already do: the 2025 Stack Overflow survey had Windows leading for professional work at 49.5 percent, but Ubuntu wasn't far behind at 27.7 percent. So less "begin," more "enthusiastically continue." ®

Pakistani pilots and cabin crew are barred from serving on flights entering Israeli airspace under new restrictions, according to media reports, after a hijacking attempt last month on a flight travelling from the UAE to Israel, in which Indian Captain Smit Machchhar was injured while foiling the suspected plot.

articles.title: Postgres 19 delayed after AI reviewers find more bugs than humans can fix
articles.text: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group has delayed the release of PostgreSQL 19, the latest iteration of the popular open source database, and held back an unusual number of features. Once slated for release in late September or early October, PostgreSQL 19 is now expected to be generally available around November 19. Developers have also dropped between eight and 10 significant features. Explaining the number of reverts — features whose rollouts have now been postponed to next year's release, PostgreSQL 20 — Peter Eisentraut, veep at EDB, a PostgreSQL support and consultancy, said the reason could be at least in part attributed to the LLM code reviews used by developers. In a blog post, Eisentraut, who is a leading PostgreSQL committer, said some of the reverted features had significant architectural defects that would have been hard to fix "quickly and during beta." However, the introduction of LLM-assisted code review also uncovered a long tail of “relatively harmless issues involving various edge cases” which, in past times, developers might not have noticed until much later, most likely issuing bug fixes in the five years following launch. “With LLM-assisted code review, these kinds of things can get found much faster, and then you’re staring at a list of forty defect reports. Even if each of them requires only a three-line fix on average, there is a fixed overhead to dealing with each of these, and then you run out of time.” When the big updates for PostgreSQL 19 were written, LLM-assisted code review was not as useful as it is now, we're told, but in the months leading up to the launch, the AI-supported reviews became better understood and more effective. “The effective quality bar has been raised after the time the feature was written and committed. Unless the capabilities of LLM-assisted code review keep improving at the current rate, this situation should sort itself out for future development cycles,” Eisentraut said. He was also at pains to point out that the reverts were not down to “vibe coding” in development, as the technique was not available when most of the new features were written. Postgres was first proposed by Michael Stonebraker in 1986. In 1994, Andrew Yu and Jolly Chen replaced the query language POSTQUEL with SQL, and in 1995 made the database freely available and modifiable under a more permissive license, renaming it PostgreSQL. It has since become the most popular database among professional developers owing to the services the big three hyperscalers built on it as well as the range of wire-compatible distributed systems available. Among the features pulled from the PostgreSQL 19 iteration is support for SQL Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ), which became part of the SQL standard in 2023. The feature provides syntax for exploring relationships between nodes connected by edges. PostgreSQL's implementation was removed over unresolved issues. At the time, PostgreSQL contributor Tom Lane warned: "At this point I'd be willing to bet dinner that if we ship it in v19 there will be post-release bug discoveries that are unfixable until v20." Despite the delay, Eisentraut promises PostgreSQL 19 will still be “a great release,” that includes REPACK CONCURRENTLY, which avoids the table-lock VACUUM FULL operation used to reclaim disk space. “And it will be very robust, after all the additional scrutiny,” he said. The features reverted from PostgreSQL 19 will likely make it into PostgreSQL 20. Just a few months ago, developers expected PostgreSQL 20 to have no new features, just bug fixes. Now, it is likely to have the new features left over from the earlier release, Eisentraut said.®
